questions.stem: How does photographic film indicate radiation exposure?

options.text: it darkens as it absorbs radiation
options.explanation: More absorbed radiation means a darker developed film.

options.text: it changes colour to blue only
options.explanation: Darkening, not a specific blue, is the signal.
Warming is not the detection mechanism.
Clicks belong to the GM tube.

questions.stem: What does a Geiger-Müller tube do each time it absorbs radiation?

options.explanation: Nothing is stored; each event is counted.

options.text: transmits an electrical pulse to a counting circuit
options.explanation: Each absorption generates one pulse — the count.
That is the film badge’s job.
The tube detects; it does not emit.

questions.stem: A GM tube is moved closer to a source. What happens to the count rate?

options.text: it stays constant regardless of distance
options.explanation: Geometry matters — the syllabus says so.
Closeness maximises, not zeroes, the count.
Closeness raises the intensity of radiation reaching the tube.
Falling is what happens when you move away.

questions.stem: Why do radiographers wear film badges with layered absorbers?

options.explanation: Weight is not the design goal.

options.text: to make the film develop faster
options.explanation: Development speed is unrelated.
A badge monitors; it does not shield.

options.text: the layers discriminate the dose delivered by different radiation types
options.explanation: Absorber layers let the developed film separate contributions.

questions.stem: Which detector gives an immediate count rate rather than a cumulative record?

options.explanation: The tube counts events as they arrive.
Film integrates until it is developed.
A box is shielding, not a detector.
Absorbers modify radiation; the tube measures it.

questions.stem: Name two detectors of ionising radiation.
questions.modelAnswer: Photographic film and the Geiger-Müller tube both detect ionising radiation.

questions.stem: State what is meant by count rate.
questions.modelAnswer: The count rate is the number of radiation detections per unit time recorded by a detector such as a GM tube.

questions.stem: Explain why a film badge is checked regularly even though it gives no immediate reading.
questions.modelAnswer: The badge accumulates darkening with every exposure, so regular checks read off the cumulative dose and flag over-exposure even though no single moment is timed.

questions.stem: A GM tube records 480 counts in 2 minutes. Calculate the count rate in counts per second.

options.explanation: Chlorine is not the named natural source.
Radon seeps from rocks and building materials.

questions.stem: Cosmic rays reaching the atmosphere produce which radiation on collision with air molecules?

options.explanation: Sound is irrelevant to cosmic rays.

options.explanation: Suffocation is not the named mechanism.

options.text: because its alpha emissions act directly inside the lungs

Radon is colourless and odourless.
The hazard is inhalation, not food contamination.

questions.stem: Define background radiation.
questions.modelAnswer: Background radiation is the ionising radiation present all around us at all times, from natural and artificial sources.

questions.stem: List three natural sources of background radiation.
questions.modelAnswer: Radon gas from rocks and buildings, cosmic rays from space, and radioactive material in food and drink (with carbon-14 in living matter).

questions.stem: Explain why radon levels differ noticeably from one location to another.
questions.modelAnswer: Radon comes from radioactive elements in rocks and soils, and geology varies regionally, so the gas seeping into buildings varies too.

questions.stem: A patient is worried that all background radiation is man-made. Give a short, evidence-based correction.
questions.modelAnswer: Most significant contributions are natural — radon from rocks, cosmic rays from space, and traces in food and drink — while man-made additions (medicine, fallout, accidents) exist but are not the whole picture.

questions.stem: The background count is 24 counts per minute. Express that per second.

options.explanation: Wrong factor of ten.
That would be 14.4 per minute.
That skips the division by 60.

questions.stem: A source gives 285 counts per minute; background is 24. The corrected count rate is…

options.explanation: Addition is the wrong operation.
That ignores the background subtraction.
That is the background itself.

questions.stem: Which is an artificial source of background radiation?

options.explanation: Medical uses of radiation add to background.
Radon is natural.
Cosmic rays are natural.
Carbon-14 is natural.

questions.stem: Why does averaging repeated counts improve the accuracy of a corrected count rate?

options.explanation: Background is steady over a session.

options.text: because the randomness of decay makes single counts scatter
options.explanation: Averaging tames the random fluctuation.

options.text: because the source weakens while you count
options.explanation: That is a real effect but not the averaging rationale asked for here.

options.text: because the GM tube drifts between readings
options.explanation: Tube drift is not the named cause.

questions.stem: Background is measured at 24 cpm. With the source at 1 m the reading stays at 24 cpm. What is the corrected count rate, and what does it mean?

options.explanation: Addition is meaningless here.
Corrected rates are not double-subtracted.

options.text: 0 — the source’s radiation is fully absorbed by the air before the tube
options.explanation: The reading equals background, so the source contributes nothing at that distance.
The 24 is entirely background here.

questions.stem: Describe how to find the corrected count rate of a source.
questions.modelAnswer: Measure the background count rate with no source present, measure the rate with the source present, and subtract the background from the source reading.

questions.stem: Give the corrected count rate in counts per second for a source reading of 261 counts per minute.
Explain why the background measurement must be taken in the same place as the source measurements.
questions.modelAnswer: Background varies with location, so a baseline measured elsewhere would not match the contributions present during the source readings, corrupting the subtraction.

questions.stem: A GM tube records 160 counts in 5 minutes with no source, and 208 counts in 5 minutes with a source. Find both rates and the corrected count rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Background: 160 ÷ 5 = 32 cpm; with source: 208 ÷ 5 ≈ 41.6 cpm; corrected: 41.6 − 32 = 9.6 cpm.
